 25: 
 26: Turn logging
 27: - Every user request (including messages queued mid-turn) is exactly one turn; actions and decisions map to the turn of the request that caused them, determined by the write-attribution rule below (D2). Enforcement of turn-logging correctness is Phase A and ships first.
 28: - Plugin turn edits are independent: opening, editing, closing, or canceling one turn never changes another turn's local or server state; concurrent edits to different turns do not interfere.
 29: - Request identity (operator D1, 2026-10-09: "have the server issue a request token when a message arrives"): the server mints every turn's `requestId` when a user message arrives (ingress), through the new mint operation `POST /qbrainai/sessionlog/{agent}/{sessionId}/mint`. The mint call carries an idempotency nonce derived from the host's own identity for that message event (host binding table): a host per-prompt id, or a SHA-256 of host event fields that every delivery of that event carries identically. Every delivery of one event therefore sends the same nonce and receives the same token, including two hook processes started by a doubly registered hook, network retries, and failsafe replay; two separate user messages (including two intentionally identical prompts) are two events and receive two tokens. On copilot and classic cline, whose event fields include no per-message id, a message whose session, timestamp, and prompt all equal an already minted one is indistinguishable from a redelivery of it, so the host session fails closed under D6 instead of merging or guessing (host binding table, equal-field rule). The host id is only the idempotency key; the turn identity is the server-issued token. There is no prompt-text dedupe window. Every mint comes from a host arrival mechanism (a prompt hook, the arrival bridge, or a host-native hook adapter); no supported host relies on the model to mint. The stop gate's `duplicate_delivery_suspected` warning is a diagnostic only and is never counted as D1 compliance.
 30: - Queued-message arrival (operator D5, 2026-10-09: "Arrival bridge"): a message the operator sends while a turn is running is minted when it is enqueued, not when the model later processes it. On hosts that record the enqueue in a transcript (Claude Code), a per-host-session arrival bridge started by the SessionStart hook tails the transcript and follows each queued message through the lifecycle the transcript records. Observed in this workspace's Claude Code transcripts on 2026-10-09: 117 `enqueue`, 79 `dequeue`, 35 `remove` (27 with reason `absorbed_mid_turn`), 2 `popAll`; a normal prompt is `enqueue` then `dequeue` within milliseconds, a mid-turn message is `enqueue` then `remove` with `absorbed_mid_turn` when it is injected into the running turn (for example the operator's mid-turn message beginning "write a global memory with the" was removed with `absorbed_mid_turn` at 2026-10-09T14:35:47.730Z), and `popAll` pulls queued text back into the input box. The bridge mints at `enqueue` (state `queued`); the request becomes `delivered` at `dequeue` (applied by the bridge from the transcript itself; on hosts with a bridge the prompt hook neither mints nor claims) or at `remove` with `absorbed_mid_turn`; it becomes `withdrawn` at `popAll` or a `remove` with any other or no reason. Task notifications and other system events that the host also enqueues are classified and never minted; on bridge hosts they keep their queue position (`kind: system`), so their `dequeue` never delivers a user request.
 31: - Hosts without an arrival mechanism (operator D6, 2026-10-09: "Adapters or unsupported"): every host gets an arrival adapter wherever the host offers any mechanism (prompt hook, transcript enqueue record, host-native hook, message-queue event). A host with no arrival mechanism is declared unsupported for turn logging until it gains one: its plugin reports `turn_logging_unsupported` on every session-log verb and writes nothing, and no first-sight minting is used anywhere.
 32: - Plugin equivalence (operator D7, 2026-10-09, confirmed in chat "1 yes" for the requirement and its qualification posted by Codex in `MEMORY-PROCESS-007` at 17:48:48Z and 17:52:06Z): all QBrain.AI plugins keep equivalent functionality; shared capabilities, contracts, fixes, and behavior changes go to every plugin; host-specific adaptations preserve equivalent supported behavior; equivalence is limited by what each host's plugin infrastructure can support, no extraordinary effort is spent forcing unworkable equivalence, and each such limit is documented as a feature-specific capability limitation instead of being claimed as equivalent. A D6 `turn_logging_unsupported` host is such a documented limitation. The limitations live in `docs/AGENT-PLUGIN-FEATURE-MATRIX.md` (one row per plugin and feature: supported, adapted, or limited, with the reason and the receipt), updated in A9 and S11 and checked by a docs contract test.
 33: - Ninth plugin (operator D8, 2026-10-09: "2 yes"): `mcpserver-grok-bot-plugin` is in scope like the other eight.
 34: - Write attribution (operator D2, 2026-10-09: tie each write to its request automatically through the agent app's hooks): every verb invocation is bound to one request automatically from host context, without the model naming it: the binding is the write target of the invoking host session at the moment the invocation starts, captured once and stored immutably with that invocation (its persist record and failsafe record), so a later message never retargets an invocation already started. A host session's write target is the request most recently delivered to the model in that host session: a prompt the host hands to the model as a new turn (the prompt hook on hosts without a bridge, or the bridge's `dequeue` delivery), or a queued message absorbed into the running turn (`absorbed_mid_turn`). Minting alone never moves the write target, so work the model is still doing for request R1 after R2 is enqueued stays on R1 until R2 is delivered. Explicit `requestId` remains accepted as an override, for example to continue R1 work after R2 was absorbed, and it is required while two or more delivered requests are open in the host session (D9). Attribution therefore maps each write to the request most recently delivered to the model in its host session when the write started. A write is never attributed by guesswork: when a verb cannot read its host session key from its own invocation context (host binding table), it binds only if exactly one live host session of its agent exists in the workspace (warning `host_session_inferred`); with none it is refused (`host_session_unknown`), and with more than one it is refused (`host_session_ambiguous`), in both cases unless it carries the trusted recovery or review-backfill pair (original MCP `sessionId` and `requestId`, verified against the server for this workspace and agent, C5); an explicit `requestId` alone never lets a verb without a host session key write. While two or more delivered requests are open (for example R2 absorbed mid-turn while R1 is still open), a write without an explicit `requestId` is refused with `request_ambiguous`, naming the open requests; the model passes `requestId` until all but one are closed.  39: Request class
 40: - Turn scalar `requestClass`: `Code` | `Docs` | `Chore` (case-insensitive in, canonical PascalCase out, anything else rejected). Required, enforced at transition to `completed` or `failed`, not at creation (hooks create turns before the agent can classify). Legacy rows backfilled to `Unclassified` (readable; never accepted on new writes from agent surfaces).

 42: Review record (shared by `agentReview` and `hostileReview`)
 43: - Fields: `status` (`Unnecessary` | `Unstarted` | `Running` | `Pass` | `Fail` | `Other`), `otherNotes`, `correctness`, `completeness` (lossless decimal 0..1), `correctnessThreshold`, `completenessThreshold` (server-stamped, read-only), `reasons` (string[]), `reviewer`, `reviewedAt` (UTC), `requestJsonlPath`, `responseJsonlPath`. No `passed` bool.
 44: - One record per kind per turn; latest write wins.
 45: - Server creates both at turn creation as `Unstarted`. `hostileReview` flips to `Unnecessary` when `requestClass` becomes `Chore`, and back to `Unstarted` if the class changes away while still `Unnecessary`. Records past `Unstarted`/`Unnecessary` are never auto-changed. Legacy turns are backfilled `agentReview=Unstarted`, `hostileReview=Unstarted`.
 46: - `otherNotes` with text is rejected unless `status` is `Other`.
 47: - Strict per-status fields: `Unnecessary`/`Unstarted` carry no scores, reasons, reviewer, timestamps, or paths; `Running` requires `reviewer`, forbids scores; `Pass`/`Fail` require `correctness`, `completeness`, `reviewer`, `reviewedAt`; `hostileReview` `Pass`/`Fail` also require `requestJsonlPath` and `responseJsonlPath`; `Other` requires non-empty `otherNotes` (the Other reason; operator D4, 2026-10-09: "Other requires Other Reason be populated") and allows optional scores, `reasons`, `reviewer`, `reviewedAt`, and receipt paths. `Unnecessary` is server-managed only.
 48: - Thresholds: `Mcp:SessionLog:ReviewThresholds:{Agent|Hostile}:{Correctness|Completeness}` (decimal 0..1, per instance through `McpInstanceResolver` overrides), default 0.98, inclusive (score >= threshold passes). Pass requires both scores to meet their thresholds. The server derives `Pass`/`Fail`; a supplied `Pass`/`Fail` that contradicts the derivation is rejected (422 `review_status_conflict`); omitting status lets the server derive it. `Other` is never derived. Thresholds in force are stamped on the record.
 49: - Names stay `correctness`/`completeness`. HV tooling maps `accuracy` -> `correctness` and integer percent -> decimal/100.

 78: Host binding table (locks the D1 nonce source, the D5 arrival source, and the D2 host session key per host; every turn token is still minted by the server). Rules common to all hosts:
 79: - Nonce: computed from the event itself, never from the hook process, so every delivery of one event yields the same nonce; a value outside `^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$` is replaced by the 64 lowercase hex characters of its SHA-256. Equal-field rule (copilot and classic cline, whose nonce hashes event fields with no per-message id): under `turn-open.lock`, a new prompt-hook invocation whose nonce already has a failsafe mint record or a `pending-<nonce>` turn in that host session, or whose mint returns `merged`, cannot be told apart from a separate message with equal session, timestamp, and prompt, so it mints and binds nothing and the host session fails closed under D6 exactly as the bridge does for an unattributable record (`unsupportedSince: { causeNonce, causeOperation: prompt_hook, reason: indistinguishable_arrival }` with the session-level envelope; every session-log verb then reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and writes nothing until the session ends, and its open turns are listed at the next SessionStart). A network retry or failsafe replay of a stored mint record is a drain of that record, not a new invocation, and reuses its nonce without failing closed.
 80: - Host session key: read from the verb's own invocation context as listed per host. Long-lived processes (stdio MCP servers, the arrival bridge itself) never trust a key captured at spawn time, because a host may change the session in place (Claude Code `/clear`; resume without an explicit id keeps the startup id in long-lived subprocesses per the Claude Code env-var reference); they resolve the key per call by the live-session rule.
 81: - Queued-message arrival on every host (D5, D6): P0.2 records, per host, whether a message sent while a turn is running reaches an arrival mechanism at enqueue. Where the prompt event itself fires at enqueue, it is the arrival mechanism; where it fires only at processing time, the host's transcript or queue event is used through an arrival adapter with the same `queued`/`delivered`/`withdrawn` lifecycle as the Claude Code bridge; where neither exists, the host is unsupported for turn logging (`turn_logging_unsupported`).
 82: - Live-session rule (D2 fallback): a host session is live from its first mint until its session-end event (Claude Code `SessionEnd`, including reason `clear`; Codex `SessionEnd`; Copilot session end; cline-v2 and opencode session close) marks `sessions/<key>/ended.yaml`, or until 12 hours without a mint or verb (the idle rule writes `ended.yaml` with `reason: idle`; a session-end event writes `reason: session_end`). A verb without its own key binds to the single live session of its agent in the workspace (`host_session_inferred`), and is refused with `host_session_unknown` (none live) or `host_session_ambiguous` (several live) unless it passes the trusted (MCP `sessionId`, `requestId`) pair of C5.
 83: - claude-code: nonce: the bridge's `q-` enqueue nonce (the bridge is the only minter, FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009); hook key payload `session_id`; verb key env `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` read at verb start in shell, PowerShell, and hook subprocesses (equals `session_id`; those subprocesses see the updated value after `/clear`); stdio MCP verbs use the live-session rule; payloads carrying `agent_id` are subagent events (system events, no turn); the subagent's own Bash and PowerShell verbs carry the parent's `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` and bind to the parent's write target; stop uses payload `stop_hook_active`. Arrival bridge (D5), the only minter on claude-code (known-good single source of truth: the host transcript is one ordered log written by one producer, so the bridge needs no key shared with the hook, which the host does not provide: Claude Code's `queue-operation` records carry no `promptId` although its user records do): started by SessionStart with the payload `transcript_path`, it applies `queue-operation` lines in file order. Every `enqueue` takes a queue position, so FIFO `dequeue` stays exact. An `enqueue` whose `content` the system-event classifier marks as a system event is added as `{ kind: system, enqueueOffset, enqueueTimestamp, promptSha256, state: queued }` with the session-level envelope `{ workspacePath, agent, mcpSessionId, hostSessionKey }` (it has no nonce or requestId, and none is ever invented for it) and is never minted. An `enqueue` whose `content` the classifier accepts as a user request: mint with nonce `q-` + SHA-256(`session_id` LF the record's starting byte offset in the transcript LF enqueue `timestamp` LF `content`) truncated to 62 hex characters (the offset is unique per record and identical on replay, so two distinct records with equal timestamp and content get two nonces), and add `{ kind: request, requestId, nonce, enqueueOffset, enqueueTimestamp, promptSha256, state: queued, stateOffset, mintedAtUtc }` with the root-id envelope to the queue in `sessions/<key>/turn-state.yaml`. `dequeue` (no content) removes the head of the host session's `queued` entries: a `kind: request` head becomes `delivered` and the write target; a `kind: system` head is removed and delivers nothing. `remove` and `popAll` records that match a `kind: system` entry drop it without a turn. `remove` with reason `absorbed_mid_turn`: the `queued` entry whose `promptSha256` equals the record's `content` hash (both written by the same producer) becomes `delivered` and the write target when exactly one queued entry has that hash. `remove` with any other or no reason: the matching `queued` entry becomes `withdrawn` when exactly one queued entry has that content hash. `popAll`: when, for every content line it carries, the number of lines with that content equals the number of queued entries with that content hash, those entries become `withdrawn`. Fail-closed rule (D6): a `remove` carries `commandUuid` and `deliveryId` (Claude Code 2.1.293), which also appear on the delivered message's `queued_command` attachment, but `enqueue` and `dequeue` carry no key shared with it, so a `remove` that matches two or more queued entries, or a `popAll` that carries fewer lines of a content than there are queued entries with that content, cannot be attributed (a `popAll` whose line count equals the matching entry count withdraws them all, because every candidate is withdrawn). The bridge never guesses: at the first such record it stops before it without advancing `appliedThroughOffset`, sets `turn-state.yaml` `unsupportedSince: { causeOffset, causeOperation, reason: queue_removal_ambiguous }`, and from then on every session-log verb in that host session reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and writes nothing until the session ends. Turns that are open at that moment are left exactly as they are on the server, the stop gate warns `queue_removal_ambiguous` listing them, and the next SessionStart for the agent lists them with their original (MCP `sessionId`, `requestId`) pairs for closing through the trusted recovery flow (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-005-AC006). P0.2 records the `remove` identity fields; the bridge never uses them to pair with an `enqueue`. Only `queue-operation` lines are arrival records; every other record type is ignored by design. A `queue-operation` with an unknown operation or a missing required field is never skipped: the bridge stops before it without advancing `appliedThroughOffset`, records warning `arrival_bridge_format_unrecognized`, and the host session reports `turn_logging_unsupported` on every session-log verb (D6) until a verified adapter handles that shape. Each record's state change and the advance of `appliedThroughOffset` past it are one atomic replace of `turn-state.yaml` (temp file, flush, rename, under `turn-open.lock`); records that start below `appliedThroughOffset` are skipped, so a restart never re-applies a record; the server mint for `enqueue` happens before that replace and is idempotent (same nonce, `merged`). Records are applied by whichever process holds `turn-open.lock`: the bridge, or a session-log verb, which first records the transcript length at the moment the invocation starts and, after taking the lock, applies every pending record that ends at or before that length, never a record appended later, before it binds (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-007-AC006), so a verb started after a `dequeue` line was written binds to that request, and a `dequeue` appended after the verb started never retargets it (D2). The prompt hook on claude-code and claude-cowork neither mints nor claims; it classifies system events and starts no turn. P0.2 verifies that every user prompt (in each prompt form of FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009) produces an `enqueue` record and that `dequeue` always takes the head; if either fails, claude-code is `turn_logging_unsupported` (D6) until an adapter with a traceable key exists, recorded in the feature matrix.

 79: - Nonce: computed from the event itself, never from the hook process, so every delivery of one event yields the same nonce; a value outside `^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$` is replaced by the 64 lowercase hex characters of its SHA-256. Equal-field rule (copilot and classic cline, whose nonce hashes event fields with no per-message id): under `turn-open.lock`, a new prompt-hook invocation whose nonce already has a failsafe mint record or a `pending-<nonce>` turn in that host session, or whose mint returns `merged`, cannot be told apart from a separate message with equal session, timestamp, and prompt, so it mints and binds nothing and the host session fails closed under D6 exactly as the bridge does for an unattributable record (`unsupportedSince: { causeNonce, causeOperation: prompt_hook, reason: indistinguishable_arrival }` with the session-level envelope; every session-log verb then reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and writes nothing until the session ends, and its open turns are listed at the next SessionStart). A network retry or failsafe replay of a stored mint record is a drain of that record, not a new invocation, and reuses its nonce without failing closed.
 80: - Host session key: read from the verb's own invocation context as listed per host. Long-lived processes (stdio MCP servers, the arrival bridge itself) never trust a key captured at spawn time, because a host may change the session in place (Claude Code `/clear`; resume without an explicit id keeps the startup id in long-lived subprocesses per the Claude Code env-var reference); they resolve the key per call by the live-session rule.

Where the prompt event itself fires at enqueue, it is the arrival mechanism; where it fires only at processing time, the host's transcript or queue event is used through an arrival adapter with the same `queued`/`delivered`/`withdrawn` lifecycle as the Claude Code bridge; where neither exists, the host is unsupported for turn logging (`turn_logging_unsupported`).
 82: - Live-session rule (D2 fallback): a host session is live from its first mint until its session-end event (Claude Code `SessionEnd`, including reason `clear`; Codex `SessionEnd`; Copilot session end; cline-v2 and opencode session close) marks `sessions/<key>/ended.yaml`, or until 12 hours without a mint or verb (the idle rule writes `ended.yaml` with `reason: idle`; a session-end event writes `reason: session_end`). A verb without its own key binds to the single live session of its agent in the workspace (`host_session_inferred`), and is refused with `host_session_unknown` (none live) or `host_session_ambiguous` (several live) unless it passes the trusted (MCP `sessionId`, `requestId`) pair of C5.

477: UC-1 Log each user request as exactly one turn. Actors: Operator, agent host (any of the nine), plugin hooks or tools, model. Precondition: workspace trusted (marker signature and health nonce verified). Basic flow: operator submits a prompt; on a prompt-hook or adapter host the hook classifies it as a user request, takes the turn-open lock, derives the nonce from the event (host binding table), asks the server to mint the requestId (the server opens the turn), and records the token as the host session's write target at once; on a bridge host (claude-code, claude-cowork) the arrival bridge mints from the transcript `enqueue` record (state `queued`) and the request becomes the write target at its `dequeue`, or at an `absorbed_mid_turn` removal (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009, -AC010); the request enters the stop ledger when it is delivered (at once on prompt-hook and adapter hosts; at its `dequeue` or `absorbed_mid_turn` removal on bridge hosts), never at mint; every verb the model invokes is bound automatically to the host session's write target at invocation start; model closes the turn. Alternate flows: the mint call is retried or replayed and returns the same requestId; a doubly registered hook delivers the event twice and both deliveries get the same requestId (on copilot and classic cline a second registration is refused before any mint, and a second equal-field invocation fails the host session closed under the equal-field rule); the server is unreachable and a provisional `pending-<nonce>` turn is rebound on drain; an identical prompt sent again later is a new event and opens a second turn; background event is skipped (on a bridge host it keeps its queue position as an unminted system entry, so its `dequeue` delivers nothing); operator sends a message mid-turn, the arrival bridge mints its turn at enqueue without touching the running turn or the write target, the message is delivered (absorbed into the running turn, or dequeued) and from then on, while the earlier request is still open, an unqualified write is refused with `request_ambiguous` (D9) and the model names the requestId of each write; once the earlier request is closed, unqualified writes bind to the delivered request; the operator pulls a queued message back (`popAll`) before delivery, the request is withdrawn, and the stop gate asks the model to fail it; a verb without a host session key in a workspace with two live sessions is refused rather than guessed; a subagent's hooks fire and leave this session's turns unchanged; while two delivered requests are open an unqualified verb is refused with `request_ambiguous` and the model names the requestId (D9); on Copilot with more than one MCP prompt hook registered the hook reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and mints nothing (D11); on a host with no arrival mechanism every session-log verb reports `turn_logging_unsupported` (D6). Realizes FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001, -002, -003, -007, -008; updated FR-MCP-SESSIONLIFE-001, FR-MCP-SESSIONLIFE-002, FR-MCP-REPL-010, FR-MCP-TRIAGESTORE-001.

542: ## Wire contracts (documented in P0 before tests)
543: 
544: Phase A
545: - `SessionLogSubmitResult` 201 body adds `turns: [{ requestId, outcome, storedStatus, reason }]`, `outcome` in `created|merged|skipped_terminal` (no `skipped_duplicate`; an identical resubmit is `merged` with reason `no_change`; duplicate requestIds in one submission are applied last-wins with one outcome each). MCP `sessionlog_submit` returns `{ success, id, turns }`. Status code stays 201 (late-hook snapshot protection).
546: - Plugin receipt on `skipped_terminal`: `code: skipped_terminal`, `persisted: false`, `storedStatus`, `reason`; verb returns false; exit 1; failsafe cleared.
547: - Hook statuses: new `system-event-skipped`, `turn-open-contended`, `turn-open-failed` (with reason `nonce_source_missing` or the server code); `turn-already-open` when a mint returns `merged` (same nonce).
548: - Stop gate: blocks `turn_in_progress` (any ledger or registered turn still in_progress), `session_turn_completion_gate` (after S8), failed build after edits (existing), stale session (existing); blocks `turn_withdrawn_unclosed` (a withdrawn queued request still in_progress); warns on exactly the FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-005-AC005 list; re-evaluates on every Stop, including `stop_hook_active=true`, blocking again while turns are open and recording `stop_gate_overridden_by_host` if the host stops anyway; passes with `{}` and clears closed entries. Auto-close removed. Block text: `session_turn_stop_gate: <n> turn(s) are not closed correctly:` then one line per turn `<id> (<code>): <remedy>`, then `The stop gate never closes turns for you.`; each turn's remedy accumulates every unmet prerequisite of that turn, in this order: at least one model-authored action, designDecision, or commit (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-005-AC002); `requestClass` (after S10); the terminal reviews the completion gate names (after S10, gate order); then the single close call valid for its status: `workflow.sessionlog.failTurn` with reason 'withdrawn before delivery' for a withdrawn request, otherwise `workflow.sessionlog.completeTurn` (or `failTurn` if the work failed), passing requestId <id>. Following a turn's remedy literally makes the next Stop pass for that turn, including a Code turn that lacks both model evidence and terminal reviews (`StopGate_EachRemedyFollowedLiterally_NextStopPasses`, `StopGate_CodeTurn_MissingEvidenceAndReviews_AccumulatedRemedy_NextStopPasses`).
549: - Ingress mint (D1): `POST /qbrainai/sessionlog/{agent}/{sessionId}/mint` (also `/mcpserver/sessionlog/...`), client `MintTurnAsync` and REPL `workflow.sessionlog.mintTurn` (hook and adapter callers only; no MCP tool), exactly as TR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-004 AC-005 specifies: first mint 201 `outcome: created`; same nonce in the same session 200 `outcome: merged` with the same requestId. 35: ### F-R22-01: post-prune alias return and RED propagation
37: **Plan locations:** C2 line 119; FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC008 line 200; TR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-008 AC-007 line 350; TEST-MCP-SESSIONTURN-008 line 377; A8 RED line 589; TODO implementationTask 18 and technicalDetails.
39: **Exact defect:** Round 21's ID-lookup counterexample is repaired: the permanent `lookup` retains pending/minted IDs after delivery is pruned. But the only specified storage of acknowledgment IDs is the prunable `delivery` entry. The locked `getAlias(id)` return type is `AliasRecord = { pendingId, requestId, aliasedAtUtc, acks: string[] } & RootIdEnvelope`; it must still return that record after pruning. The plan neither preserves the final `acks` nor defines the post-prune value and behavior of another idempotent `acknowledgeAlias`. An implementer must choose a return and replay rule. The new named test `aliasLookup_afterAllAcksPruneAndRestart_bothIdsResolve_noMoreNotifications` appears in TR-008 line 350 but not in the TEST-008 statement or A8 RED list, contrary to the claimed A8 RED propagation.
41: **Evidence and what-if:** Commit pending-P -> req-R with consumers C1 and C2. Both acknowledge; `delivery` (which contains `requiredConsumers` and `acks`) is pruned; restart. A reader holding pending-P can find the permanent lookup, but that entry has only pendingId, requestId, aliasedAtUtc and root IDs. The current QB integration's `AuditAliasSource.getAlias` returns `AuditAliasRecord`; `AuditAliasConsumer.enqueue` calls `getAlias`, then `applyAndAcknowledge`; `AuditOutbox.applyAlias` requires `Array.isArray(value.acks)` (`/home/sharpninja/github/cline/.worktrees/mcpserver-qbrain/plugins/core/lib-node/src/cache/audit-alias-consumer.ts:93-97`, `audit-outbox.ts:99-109,326-330`). Returning no `acks` breaks the consumer; inventing `[]` silently misstates acknowledged consumers. `acknowledgeAlias` is called again after lookup. Plan line 350 alone names the after-prune case; exact-string checks of lines 377 and 589 returned `False`.
43: **Change to PASS:** Keep an accurate final ack snapshot in the permanent lookup (or another explicitly permanent record), update it atomically before retiring delivery, define `getAlias` and repeated `acknowledgeAlias` after pruning and restart, and preserve the agreed `AliasRecord` interface. Strengthen FR-001-AC008 and TR-008 AC-007; add RED cases for both IDs, exact `acks`, repeated acknowledgment, no further notification and restart in TEST-008, A8, and TODO task 18. Sync the TODO description/technicalDetails and handoff if their alias summary changes. **Implementer edit; no operator decision** under agreed C2. An interface change would instead require a new C2 ACK from QB-AGENT-001.
45: ### F-R22-02: separate Copilot/Cline arrivals can share a nonce
47: **Plan locations:** D1 lines 29 and 78-79; Copilot host row line 86; classic Cline row line 89; FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC003 line 195; P0.2 line 170; A3 RED line 579; A9 adoption line 591.
49: **Exact defect:** Copilot derives `cp-` + SHA-256(`sessionId` LF `timestamp` LF `prompt`), with a Unix-millisecond timestamp. Classic Cline derives `cl-` + SHA-256(`taskId` LF `timestamp` LF `prompt`). Distinct user messages with the same host-session/task id, timestamp value and identical prompt have identical nonce inputs. The server must merge them under AC002, so they become one turn, contrary to D1 and AC003's two-turn guarantee at any interval. D11's one registered Copilot hook prevents duplicate hook commands; it does not distinguish two real messages. P0.2 probes two deliveries of *one* Copilot message, while A3 tests two separate payloads whose event id or timestamp differs. Neither checks equal timestamp and text for distinct events.
51: **Evidence and what-if:** Two Copilot UserPromptSubmit arrivals in the same millisecond, each with `sessionId=S`, `timestamp=T`, `prompt=P`, produce equal SHA-256 input by the plan's formula. AC002 requires the same requestId for that nonce. The plan identifies no stable per-message ID or durable arrival sequence for that case. The same counterexample applies to Cline if a task contains two such arrivals with equal timestamp precision. This is an internal counterexample, independent of current plugin implementation.
53: **Change to PASS:** Lock a traceable, durable per-arrival identity and replay rule for these hosts, or apply D6 `turn_logging_unsupported` when the host cannot distinguish separate events. State the selection in the host rows and P0.2 disposition, strengthen AC003, add same-session/same-timestamp/same-text distinct-event RED cases in A3/A9 and the corresponding TEST statements, and update the feature matrix, TODO and handoff. A hash of the same fields is insufficient. **Implementer edit; no new operator decision** because D1 requires distinct turns and D6 already authorizes unsupported capability. If the author proposes weakening D1 or promising support without a distinguishable event, that would require an operator decision between the existing D1 guarantee and that relaxation; this review does not authorize the relaxation.
R23 35: ### F-R23-01: arrival sequence does not distinguish redelivery from a separate identical event
R23 39: **Exact defect:** Round 23 adds `arrivalSeq` for each hook invocation, making two distinct arrivals with equal session, timestamp, and prompt different. The same fields are also all that identify a repeated delivery of one arrival to a new hook process. The plan promises that repeated deliveries of that event reuse one nonce, and A3 expressly tests two independent processes fed the same recorded Copilot payload opening one turn. Under the new rule, those processes allocate different sequence values and mint two turns. Conversely, reusing a sequence by matching the equal payload would collapse the separate messages that round 23 sought to distinguish. D11's one registered hook does not establish a stable event key or prohibit one registered hook from being invoked again. The pure `(host,payload)` nonce signatures also cannot both incorporate a mutable sequence and satisfy their stated equal-payload-equal-nonce contract.
R23 43: **Change to PASS:** In P0.2 determine whether each host exposes a stable event identity shared by every delivery/retry of one message and distinct for separate equal-field messages, or an earlier queue event that can carry a durable plugin-generated identity. Lock the source, nonce interface, replay lookup and negative probe in the host rows, FR-001-AC003, TR-001/TR-008, TEST-001/TEST-008/TEST-009, A3/A8/A9 RED, and the TODO description/technicalDetails. If neither traceable mechanism exists, apply already-locked D6 `turn_logging_unsupported` for that host and test zero mint/write; do not promise both invariants. **Implementer plan/TODO edit; no operator decision** under D1, D6, and D11. Weakening one-turn-per-event would instead need an explicit operator decision, which this review does not request.

R23 49: **Exact defect:** `Cline_TwoDistinctArrivals_SameTimestampSamePrompt_TwoMints` occurs **only on line 195**. The corresponding TEST statements and the A8/A9 RED lists do not name it or assign it to a host suite. The A8 tests named for repeated handlers cover cline-v2 `runId` and opencode `messageID`, not classic Cline's derived `cl-` nonce. The plan's claim that every changed AC has a named RED and green gate is therefore unfulfilled for this new host case.

# Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI

**v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
**April 2026**  
**Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

---
## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.
