29: - Request identity (operator D1, 2026-10-09: "have the server issue a request token when a message arrives"): the server mints every turn's `requestId` when a user message arrives (ingress), through the new mint operation `POST /qbrainai/sessionlog/{agent}/{sessionId}/mint`. The mint call carries an idempotency nonce derived from the host's own identity for that message event (host binding table): a host per-prompt id, or a SHA-256 of host event fields that every delivery of that event carries identically. Every delivery of one event therefore sends the same nonce and receives the same token, including two hook processes started by a doubly registered hook, network retries, and failsafe replay; two separate user messages (including two intentionally identical prompts) are two events and receive two tokens. On copilot and classic cline, whose event fields include no per-message id, a message whose session, timestamp, and prompt all equal an already minted one is indistinguishable from a redelivery of it, so the host session fails closed under D6 instead of merging or guessing (host binding table, equal-field rule). The host id is only the idempotency key; the turn identity is the server-issued token. There is no prompt-text dedupe window. Every mint comes from a host arrival mechanism (a prompt hook, the arrival bridge, or a host-native hook adapter); no supported host relies on the model to mint. The stop gate's `duplicate_delivery_suspected` warning is a diagnostic only and is never counted as D1 compliance.
79: - Nonce: computed from the event itself, never from the hook process, so every delivery of one event yields the same nonce; a value outside `^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$` is replaced by the 64 lowercase hex characters of its SHA-256. Equal-field rule (copilot and classic cline, whose nonce hashes event fields with no per-message id): under `turn-open.lock`, a new prompt-hook invocation whose nonce already has a failsafe mint record or a `pending-<nonce>` turn in that host session, or whose mint returns `merged`, cannot be told apart from a separate message with equal session, timestamp, and prompt, so it mints and binds nothing and the host session fails closed under D6 exactly as the bridge does for an unattributable record (`unsupportedSince: { causeNonce, causeOperation: prompt_hook, reason: indistinguishable_arrival }` with the session-level envelope; every session-log verb then reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and writes nothing until the session ends, and its open turns are listed at the next SessionStart). A network retry or failsafe replay of a stored mint record is a drain of that record, not a new invocation, and reuses its nonce without failing closed.
83: - claude-code: nonce: the bridge's `q-` enqueue nonce (the bridge is the only minter, FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009); hook key payload `session_id`; verb key env `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` read at verb start in shell, PowerShell, and hook subprocesses (equals `session_id`; those subprocesses see the updated value after `/clear`); stdio MCP verbs use the live-session rule; payloads carrying `agent_id` are subagent events (system events, no turn); the subagent's own Bash and PowerShell verbs carry the parent's `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` and bind to the parent's write target; stop uses payload `stop_hook_active`. Arrival bridge (D5), the only minter on claude-code (known-good single source of truth: the host transcript is one ordered log written by one producer, so the bridge needs no key shared with the hook, which the host does not provide: Claude Code's `queue-operation` records carry no `promptId` although its user records do): started by SessionStart with the payload `transcript_path`, it applies `queue-operation` lines in file order. Every `enqueue` takes a queue position, so FIFO `dequeue` stays exact. An `enqueue` whose `content` the system-event classifier marks as a system event is added as `{ kind: system, enqueueOffset, enqueueTimestamp, promptSha256, state: queued }` with the session-level envelope `{ workspacePath, agent, mcpSessionId, hostSessionKey }` (it has no nonce or requestId, and none is ever invented for it) and is never minted. An `enqueue` whose `content` the classifier accepts as a user request: mint with nonce `q-` + SHA-256(`session_id` LF the record's starting byte offset in the transcript LF enqueue `timestamp` LF `content`) truncated to 62 hex characters (the offset is unique per record and identical on replay, so two distinct records with equal timestamp and content get two nonces), and add `{ kind: request, requestId, nonce, enqueueOffset, enqueueTimestamp, promptSha256, state: queued, stateOffset, mintedAtUtc }` with the root-id envelope to the queue in `sessions/<key>/turn-state.yaml`. `dequeue` (no content) removes the head of the host session's `queued` entries: a `kind: request` head becomes `delivered` and the write target; a `kind: system` head is removed and delivers nothing. `remove` and `popAll` records that match a `kind: system` entry drop it without a turn. `remove` with reason `absorbed_mid_turn`: the `queued` entry whose `promptSha256` equals the record's `content` hash (both written by the same producer) becomes `delivered` and the write target when exactly one queued entry has that hash. `remove` with any other or no reason: the matching `queued` entry becomes `withdrawn` when exactly one queued entry has that content hash. `popAll`: when, for every content line it carries, the number of lines with that content equals the number of queued entries with that content hash, those entries become `withdrawn`. Fail-closed rule (D6): a `remove` carries `commandUuid` and `deliveryId` (Claude Code 2.1.293), which also appear on the delivered message's `queued_command` attachment, but `enqueue` and `dequeue` carry no key shared with it, so a `remove` that matches two or more queued entries, or a `popAll` that carries fewer lines of a content than there are queued entries with that content, cannot be attributed (a `popAll` whose line count equals the matching entry count withdraws them all, because every candidate is withdrawn). The bridge never guesses: at the first such record it stops before it without advancing `appliedThroughOffset`, sets `turn-state.yaml` `unsupportedSince: { causeOffset, causeOperation, reason: queue_removal_ambiguous }`, and from then on every session-log verb in that host session reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and writes nothing until the session ends. Turns that are open at that moment are left exactly as they are on the server, the stop gate warns `queue_removal_ambiguous` listing them, and the next SessionStart for the agent lists them with their original (MCP `sessionId`, `requestId`) pairs for closing through the trusted recovery flow (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-005-AC006). P0.2 records the `remove` identity fields; the bridge never uses them to pair with an `enqueue`. Only `queue-operation` lines are arrival records; every other record type is ignored by design. A `queue-operation` with an unknown operation or a missing required field is never skipped: the bridge stops before it without advancing `appliedThroughOffset`, records warning `arrival_bridge_format_unrecognized`, and the host session reports `turn_logging_unsupported` on every session-log verb (D6) until a verified adapter handles that shape. Each record's state change and the advance of `appliedThroughOffset` past it are one atomic replace of `turn-state.yaml` (temp file, flush, rename, under `turn-open.lock`); records that start below `appliedThroughOffset` are skipped, so a restart never re-applies a record; the server mint for `enqueue` happens before that replace and is idempotent (same nonce, `merged`). Records are applied by whichever process holds `turn-open.lock`: the bridge, or a session-log verb, which first records the transcript length at the moment the invocation starts and, after taking the lock, applies every pending record that ends at or before that length, never a record appended later, before it binds (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-007-AC006), so a verb started after a `dequeue` line was written binds to that request, and a `dequeue` appended after the verb started never retargets it (D2). The prompt hook on claude-code and claude-cowork neither mints nor claims; it classifies system events and starts no turn. P0.2 verifies that every user prompt (in each prompt form of FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009) produces an `enqueue` record and that `dequeue` always takes the head; if either fails, claude-code is `turn_logging_unsupported` (D6) until an adapter with a traceable key exists, recorded in the feature matrix.

<skill name="refresh-docs" args="then">
# Refresh Docs

Reconcile `docs/` with the current codebase, remove documentation that no longer applies, make `docs/wiki.yaml` list every project doc that should be published to the wiki, and export the MCP-backed requirement documents.

## Preconditions

- Work from the repository root.
- Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` and follow its marker, plugin, session, and trust rules. Verify the marker signature and the `/health` nonce before any MCP mutation.
- Use the required MCP Server plugin for your agent (Claude/Codex/Grok) for requirements and export (`workflow.requirements.*`). Do not hand-author exported requirement docs or substitute raw REST.
- Use the operator's approved shell for all shell invocation (e.g. PowerShell.Mcp on Windows). Build YAML/JSON from native objects and serialize; never handwrite fragile payloads.
- Read facts from the code, not from memory. This skill refreshes and exports only; it does not commit or push (leave that to a wrap-up flow or an explicit request).

## Step 1 - Refresh project documentation

1. Inventory the docs surface: `docs/user/*`, `docs/architecture/*`, `docs/requirements/*.md`, `docs/testing/*`, `docs/*.md`, and `README.md` (adapt to the repo's actual layout).
2. Establish what changed since the docs were last touched: `git log --oneline` for the changed code areas, the current project/solution structure, public commands, and settings. Prefer the shipped behavior over any doc's prior claims.
3. Update each doc that drifted: renamed or removed components, changed UI/behavior, new or removed features, install commands and version pins, and cross-references. Match the existing doc voice; no em-dashes.
4. Keep the project `README.md` current as a first-class refresh target, not an afterthought: the project description and overview, the feature list, install and quickstart/usage commands, current version references, badges, and links into `docs/` must all match the shipped state. Reconcile it against the code and the refreshed docs on every run.
5. If the repo ships a documentation screenshot/capture script (for example `scripts/Capture-ClientToolScreenshots.ps1`) and the UI changed, regenerate the embedded screenshots into the docs image folder from the current build, and verify a raw capture reflects the current UI before keeping it.

## Step 2 - Prune out-of-date docs

1. Find docs describing removed or superseded features: grep the docs for names of deleted components, APIs, or flows and confirm against the code that they no longer exist.
2. Delete the obsolete `.md` files, and remove their references from index pages (for example `docs/user/index.md`) and from `docs/wiki.yaml`.
3. Do not delete a doc that still has accurate content. When a doc is partly stale, update it rather than delete. When unsure whether to remove a doc, flag it in the report instead of deleting.

## Step 3 - Update docs/wiki.yaml

`docs/wiki.yaml` uses schema `mcp-wiki-export/v1` with `home.document`, a `documents` list, and a `navigation` tree. Each `documents` entry is `{ id, title, source, target, platforms }`.

1. Keep the server-generated requirement docs (their `source` is `generated:<key>`, for example `generated:home|functional|technical|testing|mapping|matrix`). Do not point these at files.
2. Add or refresh a `documents` entry for every CURRENT project doc that should appear in the wiki (the user guides under `docs/user/` and the architecture docs under `docs/architecture/`, plus `docs/Development-Process.md` / `README.md` if desired):
   - `source`: the repo-relative path to the markdown file, for example `docs/user/client-tool.md`.
   - `target`: the wiki page filename in PascalCase-with-hyphens, for example `Client-Tool.md`.
   - `title`: the human page title.
   - `platforms`: `[github, azure]` unless a doc is platform-specific.
   Use stable `id` slugs (for example `user-client-tool`, `arch-overview`).
3. Remove `documents` and `navigation` entries for any doc pruned in Step 2 or no longer present on disk.
4. Add each new document to `navigation` (as a child of the appropriate parent, or top-level). Keep the generated requirement docs grouped as they are.
5. If the repo has a wiki sync script (for example `scripts/Sync-GitHubWikiDocs.ps1`) with its own project-doc list, cross-check it against `docs/wiki.yaml` so the manifest and the sync script agree on which project docs publish and their page names.
6. Confirm the file still parses as YAML after editing.

## Step 4 - Export requirements

1. Export via the MCP requirements workflow: `workflow.requirements.generateDocument` with `format: wiki` and `docType: all`.
2. Write the returned `contentBase64` ZIP exactly to `docs/requirements/requirements-wiki-documents.zip`. The MCP database is the source of truth; do not hand-author the exported docs.
3. If the server also regenerates in-place markdown under `docs/Project/wiki/`, review the diff. Keep only the intended requirement changes. Do NOT accept destructive deletions of project-doc wiki pages that are listed in `docs/wiki.yaml`; that means the manifest and the export disagree, so fix `docs/wiki.yaml` in Step 3 rather than accept the deletions.
4. If the server rejects `format: wiki`, record it as a blocker and stop; do not fall back to another format unless the user asks.

## Validation and report

- Run `git diff --check`; confirm `docs/wiki.yaml` parses; if code samples in docs changed, sanity-build the relevant snippet.
- Report only verified facts: `README.md` updated, docs updated, docs pruned (with reasons), `docs/wiki.yaml` entries added/removed, screenshots regenerated, the requirements export artifact path, and any docs you flagged instead of deleting or any blockers.
- Do not commit or push; summarize the changes and let the operator run a wrap-up or commit explicitly.


**ARGUMENTS:** then
</skill>
<skill name="mcpserver:wrap-up">
Finish and synchronize MCP-backed work: reconcile requirements, export wiki documents, run validation, commit/push, and close out the session-log turn.

## Trust and transport

Trust marker details only after the plugin's local status/bootstrap check confirms marker trust and workspace health (including signature and nonce health). Use the plugin's supported wrapper surface for MCP mutations (for example `lib/repl-invoke.ps1`, or the plugin's session, todo, and requirements tools); do not use raw REST for normal MCP mutations.

## Method-name disambiguation

`workflow.*` names in this skill (`workflow.sessionlog.*`, `workflow.todo.*`, `workflow.requirements.*`) are plugin workflow/REPL method names, not literal native MCP tool names. Native `/mcp-transport` tools use names such as `sessionlog_*`, `todo_*`, and `requirements_*` (for example `sessionlog_submit`, `todo_list`, `requirements_generate`); hosted-agent adapters may expose `mcp_*` aliases. Do not declare the plugin unavailable solely because generic MCP discovery does not list literal `workflow.*` names.

If your agent exposes only a `pwsh` (or shell) tool, invoke the plugin shim directly instead of declaring it unavailable:

```
pwsh.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File "<plugin-root>\lib\repl-invoke.ps1" -Method <workflow.method> -ParamsYaml <yaml>
```

## Wrap-up steps

1. Reconcile requirements with `workflow.requirements.*`, including requirement reconciliation for new FR/TR/TEST evidence.
2. Export wiki requirements with `workflow.requirements.generateDocument` using `format: wiki` and `docType: all`.
3. Run validation commands and keep zero-failure zero-skip evidence.
4. If commit/push is required, use the `commit-sync` pause and acknowledgement contract first.
5. Perform session-log reconciliation with `workflow.sessionlog.appendDialog` and `workflow.sessionlog.appendActions`.
6. Finish with `workflow.sessionlog.completeTurn`; use `workflow.sessionlog.failTurn` when validation, export, or commit/push cannot be completed (validation failure, export failure, or blocked commit/push).

<skill name="refresh-docs" args="then">
# Refresh Docs

Reconcile `docs/` with the current codebase, remove documentation that no longer applies, make `docs/wiki.yaml` list every project doc that should be published to the wiki, and export the MCP-backed requirement documents.

## Preconditions

- Work from the repository root.
- Read `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` and follow its marker, plugin, session, and trust rules. Verify the marker signature and the `/health` nonce before any MCP mutation.
- Use the required MCP Server plugin for your agent (Claude/Codex/Grok) for requirements and export (`workflow.requirements.*`). Do not hand-author exported requirement docs or substitute raw REST.
- Use the operator's approved shell for all shell invocation (e.g. PowerShell.Mcp on Windows). Build YAML/JSON from native objects and serialize; never handwrite fragile payloads.
- Read facts from the code, not from memory. This skill refreshes and exports only; it does not commit or push (leave that to a wrap-up flow or an explicit request).

## Step 1 - Refresh project documentation

1. Inventory the docs surface: `docs/user/*`, `docs/architecture/*`, `docs/requirements/*.md`, `docs/testing/*`, `docs/*.md`, and `README.md` (adapt to the repo's actual layout).
2. Establish what changed since the docs were last touched: `git log --oneline` for the changed code areas, the current project/solution structure, public commands, and settings. Prefer the shipped behavior over any doc's prior claims.
3. Update each doc that drifted: renamed or removed components, changed UI/behavior, new or removed features, install commands and version pins, and cross-references. Match the existing doc voice; no em-dashes.
4. Keep the project `README.md` current as a first-class refresh target, not an afterthought: the project description and overview, the feature list, install and quickstart/usage commands, current version references, badges, and links into `docs/` must all match the shipped state. Reconcile it against the code and the refreshed docs on every run.
5. If the repo ships a documentation screenshot/capture script (for example `scripts/Capture-ClientToolScreenshots.ps1`) and the UI changed, regenerate the embedded screenshots into the docs image folder from the current build, and verify a raw capture reflects the current UI before keeping it.

## Step 2 - Prune out-of-date docs

1. Find docs describing removed or superseded features: grep the docs for names of deleted components, APIs, or flows and confirm against the code that they no longer exist.
2. Delete the obsolete `.md` files, and remove their references from index pages (for example `docs/user/index.md`) and from `docs/wiki.yaml`.
3. Do not delete a doc that still has accurate content. When a doc is partly stale, update it rather than delete. When unsure whether to remove a doc, flag it in the report instead of deleting.

## Step 3 - Update docs/wiki.yaml

`docs/wiki.yaml` uses schema `mcp-wiki-export/v1` with `home.document`, a `documents` list, and a `navigation` tree. Each `documents` entry is `{ id, title, source, target, platforms }`.

1. Keep the server-generated requirement docs (their `source` is `generated:<key>`, for example `generated:home|functional|technical|testing|mapping|matrix`). Do not point these at files.
2. Add or refresh a `documents` entry for every CURRENT project doc that should appear in the wiki (the user guides under `docs/user/` and the architecture docs under `docs/architecture/`, plus `docs/Development-Process.md` / `README.md` if desired):
   - `source`: the repo-relative path to the markdown file, for example `docs/user/client-tool.md`.
   - `target`: the wiki page filename in PascalCase-with-hyphens, for example `Client-Tool.md`.
   - `title`: the human page title.
   - `platforms`: `[github, azure]` unless a doc is platform-specific.
   Use stable `id` slugs (for example `user-client-tool`, `arch-overview`).
3. Remove `documents` and `navigation` entries for any doc pruned in Step 2 or no longer present on disk.
4. Add each new document to `navigation` (as a child of the appropriate parent, or top-level). Keep the generated requirement docs grouped as they are.
5. If the repo has a wiki sync script (for example `scripts/Sync-GitHubWikiDocs.ps1`) with its own project-doc list, cross-check it against `docs/wiki.yaml` so the manifest and the sync script agree on which project docs publish and their page names.
6. Confirm the file still parses as YAML after editing.

## Step 4 - Export requirements

1. Export via the MCP requirements workflow: `workflow.requirements.generateDocument` with `format: wiki` and `docType: all`.
2. Write the returned `contentBase64` ZIP exactly to `docs/requirements/requirements-wiki-documents.zip`. The MCP database is the source of truth; do not hand-author the exported docs.
3. If the server also regenerates in-place markdown under `docs/Project/wiki/`, review the diff. Keep only the intended requirement changes. Do NOT accept destructive deletions of project-doc wiki pages that are listed in `docs/wiki.yaml`; that means the manifest and the export disagree, so fix `docs/wiki.yaml` in Step 3 rather than accept the deletions.
4. If the server rejects `format: wiki`, record it as a blocker and stop; do not fall back to another format unless the user asks.

## Validation and report

- Run `git diff --check`; confirm `docs/wiki.yaml` parses; if code samples in docs changed, sanity-build the relevant snippet.
- Report only verified facts: `README.md` updated, docs updated, docs pruned (with reasons), `docs/wiki.yaml` entries added/removed, screenshots regenerated, the requirements export artifact path, and any docs you flagged instead of deleting or any blockers.
- Do not commit or push; summarize the changes and let the operator run a wrap-up or commit explicitly.


**ARGUMENTS:** then

<skill name="mcpserver:wrap-up">
Finish and synchronize MCP-backed work: reconcile requirements, export wiki documents, run validation, commit/push, and close out the session-log turn.

## Trust and transport

Trust marker details only after the plugin's local status/bootstrap check confirms marker trust and workspace health (including signature and nonce health). Use the plugin's supported wrapper surface for MCP mutations (for example `lib/repl-invoke.ps1`, or the plugin's session, todo, and requirements tools); do not use raw REST for normal MCP mutations.

## Method-name disambiguation

`workflow.*` names in this skill (`workflow.sessionlog.*`, `workflow.todo.*`, `workflow.requirements.*`) are plugin workflow/REPL method names, not literal native MCP tool names. This goal changes code. Satisfying the criteria nominally is NOT enough ΓÇö do a senior-engineer adversarial review of every file in CHANGED_FILES and the paths they touch. Read the CURRENT contents, run the code, and cite a `path:line` or a command/test transcript for every finding. Bias to `refuted: true`.

Illustrative, not exhaustive: off-by-one, wrong operator, inverted condition, wrong variable/index, null/empty dereference, unhandled error path, overflow/precision/sign, bad early-return, race.
- Completeness ΓÇö fully implement the requirement, not just the happy path. Refute when edge/error cases are silently dropped, a value is hardcoded that must be dynamic, a branch returns a placeholder, or only the demo case works.
- Real tests, not theater ΓÇö judge each test by whether it would catch a deliberately-broken implementation; one that still passes against a wrong implementation (asserts only on mocks/constants, sets internal state instead of using the real entry point, or has no meaningful assertion) is theater ΓÇö discount it (refute if it is the only evidence for a required behavior). Injecting a fake at an environment boundary (clock, RNG, network/file/output sink) so the unit's REAL logic runs deterministically is honest dependency injection, NOT theater. A green project suite is WEAK evidence, never proof. Refute hard on tests weakened, `#[ignore]`/skipped, commented out, or whose expected values were edited to match buggy output.
- End-to-end reality ΓÇö build it and exercise each behavioral criterion through the REAL entry point and observed output, judging as the USER would; driving an internal flag or helper proves the mechanism exists, NOT that the wired-up feature works. A criterion whose code is present but whose integrated behavior is wrong, unreachable, or unusable is `refuted: true`, as is anything that fails to compile, fails its tests, or errors at runtime. EXCEPTION ΓÇö behavior the harness cannot drive headlessly (a UI, a browser, a game loop, a long-running interactive session): the static/structural fallback is the accepted bar (the artifact is present AND the shipped unit-level functions ΓÇö e.g. physics, collision, input mapping, state transitions ΓÇö are exercised against the real path); this applies EVEN IF the plan did not spell the fallback out. The fallback still includes the cheap load check: a browser-loaded script must evaluate without error in a browser-like environment (`window` defined, NO Node globals) ΓÇö an unguarded `module.exports`/`require` in a `<script src>` file crashes at load (blank page) and is a decisive, headlessly-provable defect. Likewise an ES-module/import-map page with no `file:` fallback message: double-clicked from disk it is a silent black screen (CORS blocks module imports), so it must either use plain scripts or visibly tell the user to serve it. Entry-point launch: whatever the deliverable (CLI, server, library, page), it must have been LAUNCHED once on its real entry path with the cheapest runtime the environment offers ΓÇö run the command, boot the server and hit an endpoint, import the library fresh, or headless-load the page (zero page errors, plus the strong primary-observable bar below; module-resolution failures only surface on a real load).     - '- Nonce: computed from the event itself, never from the hook process, so every delivery of one event yields the same nonce; a value outside `^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$` is replaced by the 64 lowercase hex characters of its SHA-256.     - '### Use cases (new, 9)'
    - "UC-1 Log each user request as exactly one turn. Actors: Operator, agent host (any of the nine), plugin hooks or tools, model. Precondition: workspace trusted (marker signature and health nonce verified). Basic flow: operator submits a prompt; on a prompt-hook or adapter host the hook classifies it as a user request, takes the turn-open lock, derives the nonce from the event (host binding table), asks the server to mint the requestId (the server opens the turn), and records the token as the host session's write target at once; on a bridge host (claude-code, claude-cowork) the arrival bridge mints from the transcript `enqueue` record (state `queued`) and the request becomes the write target at its `dequeue`, or at an `absorbed_mid_turn` removal (FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001-AC009, -AC010); the request enters the stop ledger when it is delivered (at once on prompt-hook and adapter hosts; at its `dequeue` or `absorbed_mid_turn` removal on bridge hosts), never at mint; every verb the model invokes is bound automatically to the host session's write target at invocation start; model closes the turn. Alternate flows: the mint call is retried or replayed and returns the same requestId; a doubly registered hook delivers the event twice and both deliveries get the same requestId (on copilot and classic cline a second registration is refused before any mint, and a second equal-field invocation fails the host session closed under the equal-field rule); the server is unreachable and a provisional `pending-<nonce>` turn is rebound on drain; an identical prompt sent again later is a new event and opens a second turn; background event is skipped (on a bridge host it keeps its queue position as an unminted system entry, so its `dequeue` delivers nothing); operator sends a message mid-turn, the arrival bridge mints its turn at enqueue without touching the running turn or the write target, the message is delivered (absorbed into the running turn, or dequeued) and from then on, while the earlier request is still open, an unqualified write is refused with `request_ambiguous` (D9) and the model names the requestId of each write; once the earlier request is closed, unqualified writes bind to the delivered request; the operator pulls a queued message back (`popAll`) before delivery, the request is withdrawn, and the stop gate asks the model to fail it; a verb without a host session key in a workspace with two live sessions is refused rather than guessed; a subagent's hooks fire and leave this session's turns unchanged; while two delivered requests are open an unqualified verb is refused with `request_ambiguous` and the model names the requestId (D9); on Copilot with more than one MCP prompt hook registered the hook reports `turn_logging_unsupported` and mints nothing (D11); on a host with no arrival mechanism every session-log verb reports `turn_logging_unsupported` (D6). Realizes FR-MCP-SESSIONTURN-001, -002, -003, -007, -008; updated FR-MCP-SESSIONLIFE-001, FR-MCP-SESSIONLIFE-002, FR-MCP-REPL-010, FR-MCP-TRIAGESTORE-001."

 26: Turn logging
 27: - Every user request (including messages queued mid-turn) is exactly one turn; actions and decisions map to the turn of the request that caused them, determined by the write-attribution rule below (D2). Enforcement of turn-logging correctness is Phase A and ships first.
 28: - Plugin turn edits are independent: opening, editing, closing, or canceling one turn never changes another turn's local or server state; concurrent edits to different turns do not interfere.
 29: - Request identity (operator D1, 2026-10-09: "have the server issue a request token when a message arrives"): the server mints every turn's `requestId` when a user message arrives (ingress), through the new mint operation `POST /qbrainai/sessionlog/{agent}/{sessionId}/mint`. The mint call carries an idempotency nonce derived from the host's own identity for that message event (host binding table): a host per-prompt id, or a SHA-256 of host event fields that every delivery of that event carries identically. Every delivery of one event therefore sends the same nonce and receives the same token, including two hook processes started by a doubly registered hook, network retries, and failsafe replay; two separate user messages (including two intentionally identical prompts) are two events and receive two tokens. On copilot and classic cline, whose event fields include no per-message id, a message whose session, timestamp, and prompt all equal an already minted one is indistinguishable from a redelivery of it, so the host session fails closed under D6 instead of merging or guessing (host binding table, equal-field rule). The host id is only the idempotency key; the turn identity is the server-issued token. There is no prompt-text dedupe window. Every mint comes from a host arrival mechanism (a prompt hook, the arrival bridge, or a host-native hook adapter); no supported host relies on the model to mint. The stop gate's `duplicate_delivery_suspected` warning is a diagnostic only and is never counted as D1 compliance.
 30: - Queued-message arrival (operator D5, 2026-10-09: "Arrival bridge"): a message the operator sends while a turn is running is minted when it is enqueued, not when the model later processes it. On hosts that record the enqueue in a transcript (Claude Code), a per-host-session arrival bridge started by the SessionStart hook tails the transcript and follows each queued message through the lifecycle the transcript records. Observed in this workspace's Claude Code transcripts on 2026-10-09: 117 `enqueue`, 79 `dequeue`, 35 `remove` (27 with reason `absorbed_mid_turn`), 2 `popAll`; a normal prompt is `enqueue` then `dequeue` within milliseconds, a mid-turn message is `enqueue` then `remove` with `absorbed_mid_turn` when it is injected into the running turn (for example the operator's mid-turn message beginning "write a global memory with the" was removed with `absorbed_mid_turn` at 2026-10-09T14:35:47.730Z), and `popAll` pulls queued text back into the input box. The bridge mints at `enqueue` (state `queued`); the request becomes `delivered` at `dequeue` (applied by the bridge from the transcript itself; on hosts with a bridge the prompt hook neither mints nor claims) or at `remove` with `absorbed_mid_turn`; it becomes `withdrawn` at `popAll` or a `remove` with any other or no reason. Task notifications and other system events that the host also enqueues are classified and never minted; on bridge hosts they keep their queue position (`kind: system`), so their `dequeue` never delivers a user request.
 31: - Hosts without an arrival mechanism (operator D6, 2026-10-09: "Adapters or unsupported"): every host gets an arrival adapter wherever the host offers any mechanism (prompt hook, transcript enqueue record, host-native hook, message-queue event). A host with no arrival mechanism is declared unsupported for turn logging until it gains one: its plugin reports `turn_logging_unsupported` on every session-log verb and writes nothing, and no first-sight minting is used anywhere.

A D6 `turn_logging_unsupported` host is such a documented limitation. The limitations live in `docs/AGENT-PLUGIN-FEATURE-MATRIX.md` (one row per plugin and feature: supported, adapted, or limited, with the reason and the receipt), updated in A9 and S11 and checked by a docs contract test.

 34: - Write attribution (operator D2, 2026-10-09: tie each write to its request automatically through the agent app's hooks): every verb invocation is bound to one request automatically from host context, without the model naming it: the binding is the write target of the invoking host session at the moment the invocation starts, captured once and stored immutably with that invocation (its persist record and failsafe record), so a later message never retargets an invocation already started. A host session's write target is the request most recently delivered to the model in that host session: a prompt the host hands to the model as a new turn (the prompt hook on hosts without a bridge, or the bridge's `dequeue` delivery), or a queued message absorbed into the running turn (`absorbed_mid_turn`). Minting alone never moves the write target, so work the model is still doing for request R1 after R2 is enqueued stays on R1 until R2 is delivered. Explicit `requestId` remains accepted as an override, for example to continue R1 work after R2 was absorbed, and it is required while two or more delivered requests are open in the host session (D9). Attribution therefore maps each write to the request most recently delivered to the model in its host session when the write started. A write is never attributed by guesswork: when a verb cannot read its host session key from its own invocation context (host binding table), it binds only if exactly one live host session of its agent exists in the workspace (warning `host_session_inferred`); with none it is refused (`host_session_unknown`), and with more than one it is refused (`host_session_ambiguous`), in both cases unless it carries the trusted recovery or review-backfill pair (original MCP `sessionId` and `requestId`, verified against the server for this workspace and agent, C5); an explicit `requestId` alone never lets a verb without a host session key write. No verb ever targets the workspace-level `current-turn.yaml`.

A network retry or failsafe replay of a stored mint record is a drain of that record, not a new invocation, and reuses its nonce without failing closed.
